title: Ludwigia octovalvis: How to Spot and Control It in Rice Fields
metaTitle: Ludwigia octovalvis in Rice: Identify and Control It
metaDescription: Ludwigia octovalvis ranks fourth among broadleaf weeds of rice across the globe. Learn to spot its big yellow flowers and keep it out of your palay.
excerpt: Ludwigia octovalvis is a tall broadleaf weed with big yellow flowers that farmers call Kahoy kahoy, malapako or tina tina. It grows in irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines, and it is a special problem in dry seeded rice. This page shows you how to spot it and how to control it before it towers over your palay.

blocks.text:
In English, Ludwigia octovalvis is called Mexican primrose willow. It comes from the evening primrose family, Onagraceae. Farmers know it as Kahoy kahoy, malapako or tina tina, the same names used for its smaller cousins. Since it is a broadleaf weed, it is neither a grass nor a sedge.

You will see it in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields. Some plants act as annuals and die after one season, while others live on as perennials. It spreads by seed and by propagules, which are plant parts that can grow on their own. Left alone, a plant can reach 3 m in height, so it gets much harder to pull once it is big.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about Ludwigia octovalvis
rows: Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: This is a big, sturdy kahoy kahoy weed. It stands upright, branches out, and can grow up to 3 m tall. The stems are ridged and sometimes reddish, and the leaves are lance shaped. As a broadleaf weed, its leaves have netted veins, unlike grasses and sedges. The flowers are big and yellow, with four broad, oval petals and eight stamens. Its seed pods are larger than those of its cousins, with four angles and a reddish color.

items: Tall, branched plants that can reach 3 m and rise far above the palay.
Upright stems with ridges along their length, sometimes with a reddish color.
Big yellow flowers with four broad, oval petals and eight stamens.
Large, reddish seed pods with four angles forming along the branches.
Look alike tip: its big yellow flowers set it apart from Ludwigia hyssopifolia and Ludwigia perennis.
Thick stands in dry seeded rice fields, where this weed is known to invade.

blocks.text:
Ludwigia octovalvis is a serious weed of rice. Out of 350 weed species found in rice fields around the globe, it ranks fourth in importance among the broadleaves. It invades many kinds of rice culture, but it is a special problem in dry seeded rice.

Because it grows so tall, it shades the palay and steals the light the rice needs. It also competes for water and fertilizer. Its big seed pods add more seed to the soil each season. So the longer it stays, the bigger the stand you will have to fight next cropping.

blocks.title: Its weak spot
blocks.text: You have a free helper against this weed. The Altica beetle, a small leaf beetle from the chrysomelid family, attacks it. Its larvae and adults feed hungrily on the leaves. So when you see these beetles chewing kahoy kahoy leaves, do not spray them. Let them keep weakening the weed while you do the hand weeding.

items: Pull or cut plants while they are still short, since a plant growing toward 3 m gets tough and hard to remove.
In dry seeded rice, weed early and check often, because this weed invades dry seeded fields more than other rice cultures.
Leave the Altica beetles that feed on its leaves, and avoid needless insecticide sprays that would kill these helpers.
Cut or pull plants before the big reddish pods ripen, then bring them out of the paddy so no seed drops.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold Ludwigia octovalvis down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Ludwigia octovalvis Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Plow and harrow well, and rake out the runners, roots or pieces you turn up. A small piece left in wet soil can grow a new plant.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Ludwigia octovalvis

items.q: What is Ludwigia octovalvis called in the Philippines?
items.a: Farmers call it Kahoy kahoy, malapako or tina tina. In English it is the Mexican primrose willow. The same local names are used for other Ludwigia weeds. Even so, this one is easy to tell apart, because it has bigger yellow flowers than its cousins and can grow up to 3 m tall.

items.q: How do I control this weed in a rice field?
items.a: Start early. Prepare the land well, use clean seed, and keep water in the field where you can. Pull young plants before they get tall and tough. If you need a herbicide, choose one for broadleaf weeds that suits the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label, and spare the Altica beetles that eat it.

items.q: Why is it such a big problem in dry seeded rice?
items.a: In dry seeded rice, there is no standing water at the start to hold weeds back. So weed seeds sprout at the same time as the rice. This weed takes that chance, and it can soon tower over the young rice. That is why it ranks among the most important broadleaf weeds of rice.
